trials.notes: Correctly chose WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment() and used structural depth with next_token(). All API method names it called are present in the rendered docs. All called method names are documented, but seek('section-start-not-used') is an invalid use of the bookmark API because that bookmark was never created. That produced PHP warnings and crashed every case that reached the edit path. The traversal logic otherwise uses the right processor, depth, token type checks, and clean-scan checks, but it avoids the documented bookmark/seek pattern and ignores the failed seek.

verdict.failure_analysis: No trial chose the wrong processor; the processor-selection docs worked well here. Failed cases simple-ul, ol, existing-count-overwritten, omitted-li-closers, and nested-list-counts-direct-children share one misconception in trial-1: after walking the list contents, the candidate assumed it could still edit the list opener. In reality the cursor is on the list closer or boundary token, so set_attribute() returns false. The relevant docs are HTML Processor > Usage > Recipe: scan a region before editing its opener, which says to bookmark the opener, walk forward, seek back, then edit, and set_attribute(), which says it updates the currently matched tag. Trial-3 failed the same cases for a related bookmark misconception: it called seek() with a made-up bookmark name and no prior set_bookmark(), which the docs do not make dangerous enough and the implementation surfaces as PHP warnings. Failed cases incomplete-token-after-closed-list and unsupported-after-closed-list show the same issue under trailing bad input: the first list was fully scanned before the trailing incomplete/unsupported markup, so a bookmarked opener can still be edited. Trial-1 never returned to the opener, and trial-3 crashed on the unknown bookmark before its re-scan fallback could run. The inside-list incomplete/unsupported cases passed because the docs' paused_at_incomplete_token() and get_last_error() guidance was clear enough for the candidates to fail closed when the list scan itself was not clean.

doc_gaps.problem: It says the method updates the currently matched tag, but does not spell out the common failure mode after a subtree walk: the current token is no longer the opener the caller originally matched.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add an explicit note that set_attribute() only applies to the currently matched real opening tag and returns false on closers, text/comment tokens, virtual tokens, or after the cursor has advanced past the target. Cross-reference the bookmark/seek pattern for edits based on later-scanned content.

doc_gaps.problem: The precondition that the bookmark must already exist is not explicit enough, and the current behavior for unknown bookmarks can emit PHP warnings before returning false.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Document that callers must only seek to names previously created by set_bookmark(), should check set_bookmark()/has_bookmark()/seek() results, and that unknown bookmark names are invalid rather than a harmless no-op.

verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all 7 hidden cases, so there are no failed hidden cases to attribute to documentation gaps. The docs did well on the core contract: the HTML Processor overview says to choose `WP_HTML_Processor` for normalizing markup, and the `normalize()` section says it assumes BODY context, returns `string|null`, double-quotes attributes, adds omitted tags, and omits trailing incomplete syntax. The HTML Support section also states that unsupported markup makes output-producing methods such as `serialize()` and `normalize()` return `null`, which directly led trials 1 and 2 to the canonical implementation. Trial 3 was a near-miss in style, not behavior: it used `create_fragment()` plus `serialize()`, which the docs present as valid, but missed that `normalize()` is the simpler body-fragment shorthand. The `trigger_error` records for unsupported cases are not API misuse; they reflect `serialize()` warning while returning `null`. That warning side effect is less visible in the rendered docs than the null-return contract.

verdict.failure_analysis: All three trials passed all 7 hidden cases, with no `_doing_it_wrong` records. verdict.failure_analysis: All trials passed all 8 hidden cases, so there were no failed hidden cases to attribute to documentation gaps. The docs appear to have worked well for this task: the processor-choice guidance says to use WP_HTML_Processor when structure, containment, subtree text, or implied tags matter; the next_token()/get_current_depth() sections explain depth-bounded subtree walks and warn against nested cursor loops; the text-extraction recipe says to append only #text tokens and then call get_modifiable_text(); and the get_modifiable_text() docs state that character references are already decoded. The omitted-closers case was also supported by the docs explaining implied structure, synthesized TBODY, virtual closers, and using >= against the recorded opener depth. The only near-miss is completeness policy: none of the candidates checked get_last_error() or paused_at_incomplete_token(), but the rendered docs describe that as a caller choice for read-only extraction rather than a mandatory step.

verdict.failure_analysis: No frozen hidden case failed in any trial; all three passed 8/8. The docs did well on the central contracts: `WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment()` is presented as the right BODY-fragment parser, `next_token()` is documented for text-aware walks, `get_modifiable_text()` explicitly says decoded text is returned and must be guarded with `get_token_type() === '#text'`, and `serialize_token()` contains a near-direct wrapper rewrite example. Near-misses were limited to fallback policy and special-element over-guarding. Trial 3 followed the incomplete-token warning too aggressively by treating `paused_at_incomplete_token()` as a reason to normalize the original input, despite the `serialize_token()` section warning that `normalize()` after a rewrite discards emitted changes. Trial 2 added a redundant special-element check even though the `#text` guard already excludes SCRIPT/STYLE/TITLE/TEXTAREA opener-carried text.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs warn that `normalize( $html )` discards emitted rewrites, but models can still apply it conditionally after `paused_at_incomplete_token()` and accidentally return a successful-looking result with transformations removed.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add an explicit incomplete-trailing-token rewrite example or decision table: returning accumulated serialization preserves transformations and omits the unvisited incomplete token; normalizing the original input is a failure fallback that removes all emitted changes.

doc_gaps.problem: Special-element text handling is documented, but the sufficiency of the `get_token_type() === '#text'` guard could be even more direct. Trial 2 added a redundant `is_special()` branch after already limiting wrapping to `#text`.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short note that once code requires `#text`, comments, processing instructions, and special-element opener text are already excluded; special-element checks are only needed when intentionally opting into opener-carried text.

The rendered docs did well on the exact concepts this task required: html-tag-processor.md explains that WP_HTML_Tag_Processor is for flat, position-based attribute/class edits while WP_HTML_Processor is for structure-aware work; the Basic Usage and next_tag() sections show direct construction plus linear tag walking; the Modifying HTML attributes and remove_attribute() sections document safe attribute removal; get_attribute_names_with_prefix() documents lowercase returned names and the null case when no tag opener is matched; get_updated_html() clearly states it is the way to retrieve queued edits while preserving untouched bytes. The main adherence failure is semantic: it used a depth counter to suppress every token inside a matching `SPAN`, which deletes the subtree instead of unwrapping the boundary tags. Its incomplete-token fallback also calls `normalize($html)` on the original after a rewrite, a pattern the docs warn discards emitted changes.

Correct processor choice, no undocumented API use, and it follows the documented token-rewrite idiom: walk with `next_token()`, skip matching tag tokens, and append `serialize_token()` for everything else. It handles normalized pass-through, nested spans, attributes on removed openers, adjacent wrappers, block/void descendants, and EOF-implied closers. Minor caveat: the error fallback normalizes or returns the original input, which would discard the rewrite on unsupported markup, but it is a documented fallback choice rather than a hallucination.

Chose the right processor and only used documented methods: `create_fragment`, `normalize`, `next_token`, `get_tag`, `is_tag_closer`, `serialize_token`, and `get_last_error`. Like trial 1, it misread unwrapping as subtree skipping: once a span opener is seen, it suppresses descendant text and element tokens until the closer. verdict.failure_analysis: Trials 1 and 3 failed `simple`, `nested-spans`, `attributes-discarded`, `adjacent-spans`, `span-with-block-content`, and `unclosed-span` for one shared misconception: they treated a matched wrapper tag as a region whose contents should be skipped until its closer. The `WP_HTML_Processor::serialize_token()` section actually gives the right pattern: walking every token and concatenating `serialize_token()` reconstructs normalized HTML, and a rewrite can skip selected tokens; its example removes an element's boundary tokens while keeping contents. The phrase `Closing tokens of skipped elements must be skipped too` appears to have been read as an instruction to maintain a skip-depth and suppress descendants. Case-specific effects: `simple` lost `b c` because child tokens were suppressed; `nested-spans` lost both outer text and inner text; `attributes-discarded` correctly discarded the opener attributes but also discarded the text token; `adjacent-spans` stripped each span's text independently; `span-with-block-content` stripped text plus the child `IMG` token; `unclosed-span` exposed another missed doc point from `next_token()`: the HTML Processor emits virtual closing tokens for elements left unclosed at end of input, so the same boundary-token rule works, but a subtree skip still loses the contents before the virtual closer is reached. No trial failed because of hallucinated APIs or `_doing_it_wrong` records; the failure was an over-broad interpretation of the documented skip-token rewrite pattern.
